OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
 - $500
Define $f:\mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{N}$ by $f(n)=n/2$ if $n$ is even and $f(n)=\frac{3n+1}{2}$ if $n$ is odd.
Given any integer $m\geq 1$ does there exist $k\geq 1$ such that $f^{(k)}(m)=1$?
#1135: [La85][Er97e,p.537][La16]
number theory | 
iterated functions
The infamous Collatz conjecture. For a detailed discussion of the history and theory surrounding this problem we refer to the overview by Lagarias [La10].
This is not a problem due to Erdős; it was first devised by Collatz before 1952. Erdős referred to this problem on several occasions as 'hopeless'. As Lagarias [La16] notes, the closest Erdős ever came to working on problems of this nature is the theorem described in the remarks to [1134]. 
It is often claimed that Erdős offered \$500 for a solution to this problem; this claim originated in a survey article by Lagarias [La85].
Lagarias reported, in personal communication, that this came from a conversation he had with Erdős and Graham around 1983, in which Graham asked Erdős to make an estimate of what value Erdős would put the problem on his prize scale, to which Erdős replied \$500. Therefore, strictly speaking, Erdős never offered \$500 specifically as a prize, but we include this prize value here for comparing those problems which Erdős rated as 'prize problems'.
This is Problem E16 in Guy's collection [Gu04], in which Guy quotes Erdős as saying "Mathematics may not be ready for such problems".
Additional thanks to: Jeffrey Lagarias and Desmond Weisenberg

first accepted proof of the Collatz problem. Here is a link

 A historical comment. 
Both Erdos and Lothar Collatz were participants in the ICM 1950 in Harvard. Erdos was invited speaker, Collatz normal participant without official talk (but in the breaks he spread "his" 3n+1 problem like a salesman). 
There is a big photo online showing the whole conference group:
https://legacy-www.math.harvard.edu/history/icm1950/photos/conference2-l.jpg
On the left boarder Lothar Collatz directly right of his former boss Alwin Walther (from the wartime days at TH Darmstadt) can be seen. Here enlarged:
https://althofer.de/icm-1950-walther-collatz-2.jpg
Collatz is the egghead in the orange frame. Journalist
Annette Erbe had identified Collatz (in 2023) in that photo.
Who can identify Paul Erdos in the big (linked) photo?
Kind regards, Ingo.

 In anticipation of a large number of proposed comments to this problem, and in my capacity as a moderator for this site, let me quote two sections from the general comment policy:
"Low-value comments that I judge to be written by AI may be not shown and/or deleted at my discretion."
"Long detailed formal proofs of problems should not be posted as comments; if you have such a proof (and have checked yourself, as a human, that it is correct), you are encouraged to write it up as a preprint in the traditional fashion and submit it to a journal. There is no firm rule about what is 'too long/detailed', and this is heavily context dependent."
I will also take this opportunity to link to two of my pieces of career advice: "Don't prematurely obsess on a single "big problem" or "big theory"" and "Don't base career decisions on glamour or fame".

As such, please try to limit your comments here to the intersection of Erdős and Collatz.
